name: Blackfoot, Siksika dialect
confidence_why: Van der Mark 2003, Stacy 2004, Elfner 2006 and Frantz 1970 all describe Blackfoot prominence as a pitch-realized accent, one per word, whose position is essentially lexical, but Weber 2020 (working with a Blood-dialect speaker) and Kaneko 1999 argue that much of it is predictable from syllable weight and metrical structure, so the lexical reading is the better-supported one rather than a settled consensus.
catalog_citation: Van Der Mark, Sheena Chantal. 2003. The phonetics of Blackfoot pitch accent. MA thesis, University of Calgary. xiii+113 pp. Open PDF:https://hdl.handle.net/1880/40174(ucalgary.scholaris.ca).
catalog_quote: Blackfoot PA is primarily lexical. Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent; no words are accentless, while some words contain more than one PA. However, multiple PAs uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes. A PA can occur on either a long or short vowel. Additionally, Blackfoot has a small number of contour PAs - both rising and falling. These occur only on long vowels, with the PA associated with only one mora; the first for falling PAs, and the second for rising PAs. Syllable weight appears to interact with PA in Blackfoot, though not consistently. Kaneko (1999) notes that PA tends to fall of heavy syllables. While there are numerous exceptions to this generalization, it appears to be an active component of the Siksika grammar in that other phonological changes fall from this fact.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blackfoot is a pitch accent language: each word normally carries one lexically specified high-pitch accent (marked with an acute in Frantz's orthography) whose position is not predictable from syllable count or word edge; it may fall on a long or short vowel anywhere in the word. Tendencies reported but not rules: accent prefers heavy syllables (leftmost heavy in monomorphemic nouns, Kaneko 1999 via Van der Mark 2002:181), often sits near the left edge and avoids the right edge (Stacy 2004). Elfner 2006:14 sums up: 'accent placement in Blackfoot is virtually unpredictable, although some generalisations exist'. Frantz 1991:34, 65 (via Stacy) says the accent-assignment rules are 'poorly understood'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress in the modern accounts (culminative single PA; extra PAs in compounds are treated as multiple accents, not secondary). Uhlenbeck 1938:9-10 marks a 'secondary stress or stresses' with the grave in Southern Peigan, and says it is often impossible to decide which stress is strongest.
new_statements.exceptions: Multiple PAs in some compounds and verb complexes; contour (rising/falling) PAs on long vowels linked to one mora; weight tendency has 'numerous exceptions'. Stacy 2004:11-12, 75: ~10% of imperatives take a discourse-driven accent on the stem-final vowel; devoiced ('deficient') syllables and right-edge elements do not bear accent; some polymorphemic words surface with no accent or with adjacent accents. Uhlenbeck 1938:9 (Southern Peigan) reports 'wavering stress' and disyllables with equal stress on both syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: elicited citation forms of nouns and verbs from five Siksika-dialect speakers (ch. 5, p. 35). Frantz 1991:3 (quoted in Stacy 2004:55) notes utterance-level declination, so a late accented syllable may be lower in absolute pitch than an earlier unaccented one but remains high relative to the following syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: siks1238 is the language-level code for Blackfoot/Blackfeet (Siksika, Kainai/Blood, Piikani/Peigan, Aamsskaapipikani/South Peigan dialects). The quoted statement (Van Der Mark 2003) describes the Siksika dialect specifically (five Siksika Nation speakers, Alberta); Kaneko 1999's weight generalisations come from Blood (Kainai) speakers; Uhlenbeck 1938's expiratory-stress description is Southern Peigan (Montana, 1910s data). Frantz 1991 covers Blackfoot generally. All sources treat the accent system as shared across dialects.

Its position is not given by a fixed rule: it depends partly on vowel length (heavy syllables attract it) and partly on 'inherent' (lexically marked) stress of particular syllables, with the rules apparently also sensitive to whether the word is a verb or a noun; Frantz says the analysis of the system was incomplete.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Blackfoot has a lexical pitch accent realised as high F0; every word has at least one accented syllable. The slides restate the older view that the accent's position is unpredictable (Uhlenbeck 1938, Frantz 2009) and note that Kaneko 1999 (quantity-sensitive, culminativity, alignment) and Weber (iambic feet) claim it is largely predictable, with frequent words as counterexamples. In their own measurements of 35 two-, three- and four-syllable words from one elderly Blackfeet speaker (Chief Earl Old Person), the highest-F0 syllable was the first, second or third, never the fourth; accented syllables are higher word-initially and downdrift; long accented vowels rise toward the end or drop in the middle.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated; 'Words with multiple accents' is listed under future work (slide 38).
new_statements.exceptions: Frequent words (boy, man, baby) are counterexamples to the predictability accounts; the data set is 35 words in isolation from a single speaker, so 'first, second or third syllable' is an observation, not a rule.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence (high pitch peak, orthographic acute) is analysed as primary metrical stress computed over the Phonological Phrase: exactly one most-prominent syllable per PPh (obligatory, culminative). For verb stems at the left edge of the PPh (p. 160, (325)): monosyllable -> that syllable; disyllable -> 2nd syllable; longer -> 2nd syllable if heavy, else 3rd (quantity-sensitive iambs with the first syllable unparsed, i.e. initial extrametricality). Initial-syllable stress only when the first syllable is heavy, has a [-high] vowel and the verb is in the independent clause type (p. 160). Noun accent is lexically unpredictable (p. 46, after Weber & Allen 2012); affixes shift accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 177: PPhs sometimes carry more than one pitch accent (Frantz 2009); the less prominent ones 'could be analyzed as secondary stresses', left for future research; in tableaux secondary stresses are treated as covert (p. 166-167).
new_statements.exceptions: §3.2.2.1.3 p. 163: if the predicted (third) syllable has a voiceless nucleus, stress falls one syllable to the left (on the 2nd). §3.2.2.1.4 p. 164: several stems have idiosyncratic (lexical) stress, e.g. ihpíyiwa, i'póyiwa with light 2nd-syllable stress, isínaakiwa, and stems with initial stress in nominalizations. Stress is affected by morphological composition (prefixes), p. 156.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog entry is 'Blackfoot, Siksika dialect', but none of the three works is based on Siksiká speakers: Weber 2020's stress chapter and Weber & Allen 2012 rest on one Káínai (Blood) speaker, Beatrice Bullshields (Weber 2020 p. 157, §1.4.1 p. 26; poster acknowledgements); Prins 2019 records a Piikani (Northern Piegan) speaker and an Aamsskáápipikani (Blackfeet, Montana) speaker (pp. 23-24). All treat Blackfoot as one language with four mutually intelligible dialects (Weber 2020 p. 24-25); Van der Mark 2003 (catalog source) used five Siksiká speakers.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nominal accent is morpho-lexically determined: noun stems are either lexically accented (one syllable carries the accent, kept under prefixation) or unaccented; for unaccented stems the prefix decides whether accent falls on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable of the word (three prefix classes); third-syllable-accenting prefixes accent the 2nd syllable instead when it is heavy; every bare nominal surfaces with at least one accent (underlyingly accentless stems get a pitch fall over the last syllable pre-pausally).
new_statements.exceptions: Voiceless syllables cannot carry pitch: if accent is predicted to land on a voiceless syllable it shifts one syllable to the left (e.g. pok- + ohpoos -> pó.koh.poos). Accented roots 'generally' keep their lexical accent and are unaffected by prefixes.

sources.quote: Blackfoot PA is primarily lexical. Blackfoot words typically contain one pitch accent; no words are accentless, while some words contain more than one PA. However, multiple PAs [are] uncommon, occurring in a few types of poly-morphemic words such as compounds or verb complexes. A PA can occur on either a long or short vowel. [...] Syllable weight appears to interact with PA in Blackfoot, though not consistently. Kaneko (1999) notes that PA tends to fall o[n] heavy syllables. While there are numerous exceptions to this generalization, it appears to be an active component of the Siksika grammar in that other phonological changes fall from this fact.
sources.note: §2.2.5 p. 11: Blackfoot pitch accent (PA) is primarily lexical; one PA per word typically, no accentless words, occasional multiple PAs in compounds/verb complexes; PA on long or short vowels; rising/falling contour PAs on long vowels; weight interacts inconsistently (Kaneko: PA tends to fall on heavy syllables, many exceptions). Instrumental chapters 6-8 show F0 is the main correlate, with intensity and duration also higher on accented vowels; consultants = five Siksika-dialect speakers (p. 35).
